rv.q: It finely bring things together in a true central explanation: love is our way through chaos. And it provides the best portrait since Elena Ferrante of women together.
Mosquitoes has a lot to recommend it – not least that, for a play about science, it is very funny and very sad – often at the same time.
Like the universe itself, it’s sometimes hard to see exactly how or why ‘Mosquitoes’ works – but it does.

It’s a joy though to see a play devote this much space and time to examining what it is to be a sister, a mother and a daughter, while also contemplating the workings of the universe and our place within it.
Alas, that potentially fruitful storyline is obliterated by a mass of pseudish science stuff, delivered by a badly-shaved man in a white coat, waving his arms in the air.
The result is emotionally involving as well as intellectually satisfying.
Factor in the sizeable leaps in logic required at times by the plot, and you have an experience that exhausts at least as often as it enlightens.
This is not just a play: this is a living, breathing organism.
Mosquitoes is the classic fat play from which a thinner – far better – play is struggling to emerge.

cn.t: Kirkwood's ambitious play about feuding sisters tackles big themes like particle physics and family dysfunction with mixed results. Critics praise Olivia Colman's performance but find the work overreaching and pretentious at times.
